messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cashier
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mihai had been 76 for only a few months when he finally agreed that he could no longer manage on his own. He was a widowed cashier in a small grocery store on the edge of a Midwestern city, a place where his routine had once been simple and steady: early shift, the same customers, the same walk from the bus stop. Long before that, as a young man in a European war zone, he had been caught in a street bombardment while crossing to fetch bread for his family. He remembered the blast mostly as fragments of image: a wall splitting open, dust lifting in a white cloud, a woman’s shoe in the road, his own hands pressed to the pavement. Even now, when he spoke of it, he often drifted into a flat, distant tone, saying it was “like it happened to someone else,” yet at other moments the scene arrived with terrifying force, and he was back in the street with the sound and light returning all at once. The memory was not a story he could tell in sequence; it came as pictures, as flashes, and those flashes carried the feeling that the danger was immediate.

After the war, Mihai had tried to build a life by keeping quiet and staying useful, but over the years he came to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe. The bombardment had convinced him that danger could appear without warning, and that conviction made the images of the event more gripping whenever they surfaced. Once they did, he found himself scanning his surroundings for signs that trouble was near. In the store he watched customers’ hands, their faces, the way they stood too close to the counter. On the bus he chose a seat near the door and kept one eye on the other passengers. At night he lay awake because he felt he had to stay alert, as if sleep were a careless act that might let something happen. What frightened him most was not only what had happened then, but what the memory seemed to prove now: that the world remained dangerous and that he was no longer the capable man he had once been.

Those images also changed the way he moved through daily life. Mihai stopped driving after an episode at a traffic light when the sight of a sudden brake light and a distant bang from construction work pulled him back into the blast scene so sharply that he had to grip the wheel and wait for it to pass. Since then he avoided being a passenger as well, preferring to walk longer distances or decline invitations rather than risk the enclosed space of a car. He had come to think that staying away from driving was the only sensible choice, because once the pictures arrived he could not trust himself to remain steady. When the memories surged, he felt on guard all over again, and that tension fed his sense that he must watch everyone closely for possible harm. The more he arranged his life around staying alert, the more he seemed to confirm to himself that danger was everywhere.

Mihai’s attempts to make sense of the trauma also kept it close. He spent long evenings asking why such a thing had happened to him, turning the event over in his mind in search of an explanation or a reason, but the questions only deepened his conviction that life had betrayed him. He said he had lost his faith in people and in any higher power that might have protected the innocent, and when he thought about the bombardment in that way the memory became more than a recollection; it became evidence that no one could be trusted and that he himself was no longer capable of the sort of self-reliance that had once defined him. He had once been the man who worked, drove, made decisions, and kept his family safe. Now he felt diminished by his own startle response and by the need to check exits, sit with his back to the wall, and keep watch on the faces around him.

Over time, Mihai’s efforts to push away any feeling that seemed too warm or hopeful also narrowed his world. He no longer allowed himself to enjoy an afternoon with a neighbor or the small pleasure of a kind conversation at the register, because positive feelings seemed unsafe to him, as if lowering his guard might invite another blow. That restraint left him emotionally cut off and more certain that he was living in a hostile world. He missed his wife deeply, yet even grief felt risky because it could open the door to the images and the numbness that followed them. Sometimes he could recall the bombing and feel nothing at all, as though it had happened to a stranger; other times the street, the dust, and the sense of imminent death would come back so vividly that he felt he was in it again. Each time, the memory made him more watchful, more convinced that people could not be trusted, and more committed to keeping himself away from anything that might stir it up.

By the time he sought help, Mihai was exhausted by this narrowed life. He still went to work, but he moved through the grocery store as if through a perimeter he had to defend, and the bus ride there had become a daily ordeal. He came because the sleeplessness and constant vigilance were wearing him down, and because he feared that if he kept living this way he would disappear into fear before he truly became unable to do anything at all. What he hoped for, though he said it quietly, was not to forget the war but to be able to remember it without feeling hunted by it, and to believe again—at least a little—that he might still be safe among other people.
